previous.passage: Mangoes, mostly, though the orchard outside Surabaya had long ago given up deciding. Arisa counted eleven trees still standing and two that had lain down sometime before the rains. Thuy said the fallen ones were resting. Arisa said they were firewood with good manners. They walked the rows the way they had as girls, kicking husks, naming the trees after teachers they had disliked. At the gate Arisa took a parcel from her bag: the brass bell Thuy had mailed to her new flat in Jakarta, still in its paper, the knot untouched. Thuy looked at the knot, not at the bell. She did not ask why. Arisa tied the parcel to the lowest branch of the eleventh tree, where the wind could reach it, and stepped back. They waited. When it rang once, faintly, Thuy reached up and tightened the knot so it would hold through the season.

previous.passage: Three rules for the salt pans, Aoife had told the squad on the first morning: hats on, water every hour, no running where the crust is thin. Lanying had broken the third rule once, two years ago today, and had not played a full match since. Now she sat on the cooler with her knee strapped, timing the others' sprints with a stopwatch that ran four seconds slow. Aoife did not correct it. She read the numbers aloud as given and wrote them on her clipboard in neat columns. At noon the team left for lunch in the van. Aoife stayed. She walked out to the thin place, where the white crust had split into plates, and stood there with her hands in her pockets. Lanying came after a while, limping, and stood beside her. Neither of them mentioned the date. Aoife handed her the clipboard and the pen, and Lanying wrote one more line at the bottom of the column, below the others, in her own hand.

Devon, who rode my father's ferry every summer
and talked the whole way across about nothing,
asks me to the spring dance under the dead scoreboard.
I tell him he dances like a dropped mop.

which is not lying, exactly—

and straighten the ones he didn't,

I stand a while by the bleachers
where he left his jacket, and fold it

and carry it home on the ferry, on my lap,
the whole way across.
